processing: Fully oxidised black tea made by CTC (crush, tear, curl), which cuts the leaf into small even granules; the estate moved from orthodox to CTC in 1989.
harvest_season: Picked through the year; season-specific prized lots are little documented.
appearance_dry: Small, even, dark brown granules in grades such as BP1 and BPS.
appearance_liquor: Deep, bright red-brown, as is typical of CTC tea.
appearance_wet: Fine, even coppery particles rather than open leaf.
taste_profile: As with other high-grown CTC, expect a quick, strong, brisk cup with body; the estate's own tasting notes are little documented.

brewing.notes: CTC gives up its strength fast, so keep the steep short. It takes milk well.

vintage_note: Sold by grade through the Colombo auctions in the Western High CTC category, where it has set repeated record prices for grades including BP1 and BPS. Like other CTC, it is a tea to drink fresh, within about a year of manufacture.
description:
Dunsinane is a large estate in the Pundaluoya valley, with its factory at about 4,600 feet (some 1,400 metres), sold in the Western High category. Its distinction is unusual for high-grown Ceylon: it is a specialist in CTC rather than orthodox leaf.

CTC cuts leaf into tiny granules, so the tea brews fast and strong. Most people associate that style with low-grown or Assam tea. Doing it at this height is what has earned Dunsinane its reputation at auction.

Use less leaf and less time than you would for orthodox tea: about two and a half minutes will do. It stands up to milk and sugar, which is really what this kind of tea is for.

Look for the grade on the invoice.
history:
The estate is said to date from 1879, and covers about 790 hectares, some 494 of them under tea. The key change came in 1989, when it moved from orthodox to CTC manufacture.

It turned up in an unexpected place in the early 1970s, when US dental researchers began following Tamil tea workers at Dunsinane and Harrow in a landmark study of how gum disease progresses naturally.

A 2026 report names Elpitiya Plantations as owner and Aitken Spence Plantations as manager.
